params.name: a
params.let: s * (u + v) * (u if sw == 0 else v)

params.name: b
params.let: s * (u + v) * (v if sw == 0 else u)

params.why: keep both bases small enough to add the reciprocals by hand

solution: Use the negative exponent identity on each term: ${=a}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{{=a}}$ and ${=b}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{{=b}}$, so the denominator is $\dfrac{1}{{=a}}+\dfrac{1}{{=b}}$.
Add the fractions over their common denominator ${=L}$: $\dfrac{1}{{=a}}+\dfrac{1}{{=b}}=\dfrac{{=L // a}}{{=L}}+\dfrac{{=L // b}}{{=L}}=\dfrac{{=N}}{{=L}}$, which simplifies to $\dfrac{1}{{=ans}}$.
The whole expression is 1 divided by $\dfrac{1}{{=ans}}$, and dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal: $\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{1}{{=ans}}}={=ans}$.
The sum of two separate powers cannot be gathered into one power, so ${=a}^{-1}+{=b}^{-1}$ is not $({=a}+{=b})^{-1}$; each term is dealt with on its own.
notes: Uses the negative exponent identity on numbers, as the book's ex2-1-8 does (5 over 2^-3), but inside a reciprocal of a sum: this is the book's twist that the catalogued misconception mc:g10m2s2-1-1:power-through-a-sum describes (gathering a^-1 + b^-1 into (a+b)^-1 would give the wrong answer a + b). The bases are built as a = s(u+v)u and b = s(u+v)v with gcd(u, v) = 1, which guarantees that ab/(a+b) = s*u*v is a whole number, so 1/a + 1/b is always a unit fraction 1/(suv) and every instance has a clean whole-number answer between 2 and 12. Orientation (a, b) or (b, a) is drawn at random. Both bases are at most 40 and are never equal. Twenty distinct instances in all. Numeric answer, so no distractors; the solution's fourth step names the misconception without naming the wrong value.
